title: Hotel Phone Systems Compared: IVR, Voice Bot, Call Center, AI | Codyco
summary: A practical comparison of four ways hotels handle the phone: IVR, voice bot, outsourced call center, and resolution-focused AI. Judged on one test: does a confirmed booking land in the PMS, or does a person enter it later.
body_markdown:
## The IVR, or phone menu


**What it actually does.** An IVR is a recorded menu. It plays a list of options, reads which button the caller presses, and routes the call to the matching department, following a fixed tree that was defined in advance.


**Where it breaks.** A menu can only send a caller somewhere. It cannot answer. After reception closes, the same daytime tree still routes a caller to reservations or events desks that[went home hours ago](https://www.codyco.ai/blog/what-happens-when-a-guest-calls-your-hotel-after-hours) , and the call ends in the same silence it would have without any menu. During staffed hours it is only as good as the person it points at, and real requests do not travel in straight lines. One case from the market shows the ceiling clearly: a large budget chain ran a booking assistant built by a major technology company as a rigid decision tree, and callers who said "I have a question" got stuck in the question branch and could not get back to the booking flow, so people who actually wanted to book abandoned the call. A tree can only move a caller between branches it was told about in advance.


**Does the booking land in the PMS?** **No.** The caller is sorted, not served.


## The voice bot


**What it actually does.** A voice bot holds a conversation. It answers common questions in natural language and, when the request turns into something real, escalates to a human.


**Where it breaks.** Answering a question is not the same as resolving a request. A voice bot can talk fluently and still end every meaningful interaction with a version of "let me connect you to someone who can help," which means the transfer is the product. The hard part, writing a confirmed reservation into the system the hotel runs on, was never on the table. There is a second cost that shows up over time. A voice bot lives on one channel, so its knowledge is built for that channel and then rebuilt again for the phone, again for email, again for the next surface, and each copy drifts out of date on its own. This is also why horizontal vendors, the ones selling the same assistant into a dozen industries at once, tend to stall at exactly this point: depth in one vertical is expensive, and a platform stretched across many of them cannot afford to go deep enough in hotels to close the reservation loop.


**Does the booking land in the PMS?** **No.** The guest still needs a person to finish it.


## The outsourced call center


**What it actually does.** An outsourced call center puts a person on the line, off-site, working from a script. It answers the call, takes down the request, and promises that someone at the hotel will follow up.


**Where it breaks.** The agent cannot see the hotel. There is no live view of availability, no access to the property's own approved answers, and no way to write into the system of record, so the best an off-site desk can do is take a message and open a callback. The guest is answered and still not resolved. One operator running our system put the reason for moving away from that model plainly: the whole point of the AI, in his words, was to reduce the traffic in the call center, not in the individual department. There is also the arithmetic of delay. A booking that could be confirmed in forty seconds on the call becomes a message in a queue, a callback attempt the next day, and a follow-up call if the guest does not answer. By then the room may already be booked through a portal, and the hotel pays the commission on a guest who had already chosen it. That is the honest read on outsourcing. It relocates the call to somewhere cheaper and further away, and the guest who most wanted to feel like they were talking to the hotel is the one who notices they are not.


**Does the booking land in the PMS?** **No.** A ticket waits in a queue.


## Codyco - A system that finishes the task


**What it actually does.** This is the model built to complete the request rather than pass it on, and it is where Codyco fits. Codyco resolves the requests it can complete reliably: FAQs, straightforward bookings, confirmations, booking changes, and invoice requests. Where a booking can be completed, it reads live availability and connects the eligible outcome to the hotel's configured booking process, so the reservation is written into the system the hotel already runs. End-to-end booking workflows run in production on Sihot, Oracle OPERA Cloud, and Apaleo. The property management system stays the system of record for inventory, rates, and reservations, and Codyco is the conversational and workflow layer on top of it, working from one approved set of operational facts per property rather than a copy rebuilt for every channel. When a guest asks something the system cannot answer, Codyco flags it. The general manager gets an email showing the gap. They reply to close it. No documentation project, no separate workflow. The same path handles corrections when something in the knowledge is wrong. Before any change goes live, it is tested against anonymized real calls, so a fix for one question does not quietly break three others.


**What it will not do.** Finishing the routine work is only credible if the system also refuses the calls it should not touch. Complaints go to a person by default, group inquiries and anything that turns on authority the system does not have are forwarded to the right person, and safety-critical calls leave the normal flow through hardened safety-issue detection and go to the hotel's configured line. When the system does not know something, it says what it knows, asks a clarifying question, or hands over, because uncertainty is never turned into a confident hotel policy, and an uncertain PMS response is never presented as a confirmed booking. The full mechanics of where that line sits, and how a handover reaches a person instead of ending in silence, are covered in[a separate post on where the AI stops and the team starts](https://www.codyco.ai/blog/where-our-ai-stops-and-your-team-starts) . These are controls that reduce the risk of a wrong answer. They are not a claim that a wrong answer never happens.


**Does the booking land in the PMS?** **Yes.** That is the design requirement, not a feature added on top.
